newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia finds opposition to state firms overhaul.
newsitem.headline: Croatia finds opposition to state firms overhaul.

text.p: Croatia has achieved a good level of macroeconomic stability but is facing resistance as it presses on with state company restructuring, Prime Minister Zlatko Matesa said on Wednesday.

"On the company level, resistance is much stronger because this touches the social sphere. Old habits die hard and what one hates most are personal sacrifices," Matesa told reporters at a conference on transition economies.
He referred to a mixture of social concerns about inevitable job losses and political pressure to curtail the large expenditure needed to support ailing industries.
Matesa said an immediate priority was to create more jobs.

The government has in the past few years taken over most of the debts of state companies, built up due to war-induced losses and spiralling financing costs, to help key sectors get back on their feet.

This was accompanied by an overhaul of the banking industry which involved writing off millions of dollars of bad loans and recapitalising banks. Matesa said this process would end early next year with the largest bank, Privredna Banka.
Much of the economy is still in a fragile state, however, and parts of manufacturing industry in particular lag behind foreign competitors because of old technology and high labour costs.
However Matesa said the time had come to let companies fend for themselves despite opposition to changes.
"The goal is to make the Croatian economy competitive on the world market. But it is difficult to balance the restructuring needs against giving (the companies) time to upgrade," he said.

The government hopes to enable this by providing a stable macoeconomic framework. It has managed to keep inflation stable and the budget deficit low since strict anti-inflation measures were introduced almost four years ago.
Annual inflation ran at 3.6 percent in May, well within a 3-5 percent target set for this year. The 1997 budget deficit is projected at 2.6 percent of GDP.
